result.summary: The skill-isolation surface is well-grounded in the existing design system: it reuses the established amber warning vocabulary (--amber paired with a ⚠ glyph on both the roster badge and the section, mirroring .esc-warning / .ha-warning / .ha-notice-warn), follows the 8pt spacing tokens (--s2/--s3), uses the eyebrow/mono hierarchy correctly, and degrades to nothing when there are no findings (neutral, not an error). Status colour is never colour-alone — every amber element carries a glyph or a word ("warning" in the note). The copy is concise and sentence-case, and the warning reads as a warning, not an error, which matches the contract. The main weakness is the chosen prominent identifier: leakSkillName returns the last path segment, which for real Codex skill paths is always "SKILL.md", so the most prominent (mono, full-ink) token in every finding row is the same uninformative filename while the distinguishing skill folder is demoted to the muted, ellipsised path. There are a couple of smaller refinements around double-truncation of the snippet and a minor a11y nicety, but nothing blocks shipping.

findings.title: Prominent skill name is always "SKILL.md" — the distinguishing signal is buried
findings.detail: leakSkillName() returns the last path segment of the leak path, and that is rendered as the single full-ink, mono, flex:none lead token of every finding row (.skill-leak-name). For real Codex skills the path is ~/.codex/skills/.system/project-overseer/SKILL.md — every file is named SKILL.md, so the most prominent element in EVERY row reads the identical, uninformative "SKILL.md". The actual identity of the leaked skill (the folder, e.g. project-overseer) is demoted to the muted, single-line-ellipsised .skill-leak-path below it. The live data confirms this: the test asserts leakSkillName(...project-overseer\SKILL.md) === "SKILL.md" and getByText("SKILL.md"). On the squint test the operator cannot tell which skill leaked — and with 2 findings on the one live run both rows lead with the same word. This defeats the whole point of giving the name visual primacy.
findings.suggestedFix: Make leakSkillName climb past a SKILL.md / SKILL.* leaf to use the containing skill folder as the name (e.g. project-overseer), falling back to the last segment only when there is no parent. Keep the full cleaned path muted below for provenance. The component code does not need to change — only the helper.

findings.title: Snippet is double-truncated (160-char slice AND single-line ellipsis)
findings.detail: snippetOf() slices the cleaned snippet to 159 chars + ellipsis, and .skill-leak-snippet additionally applies white-space:nowrap + overflow:hidden + text-overflow:ellipsis. So the snippet is cut twice: first to 160 chars with an ellipsis, then visually clipped again to whatever fits one line in the 380px inspector — meaning the appended "…" from snippetOf is itself usually clipped and the operator effectively sees roughly one line regardless of the 160 budget. The 160-char cap is dead effort for the inspector width. The snippet is the only contextual evidence in this section, so giving it just one clipped line is thin.
findings.suggestedFix: Pick one truncation strategy. Either drop the JS 160-slice and let CSS single-line ellipsis own it (cleanest), or — better for an evidence line — allow the snippet up to 2 lines via -webkit-line-clamp:2 (with display:-webkit-box) and remove the nowrap so the 160-char budget is actually usable.

findings.title: Decorative ◆ severity glyph is redundant and adds visual noise per row
findings.detail: Each finding row leads with an amber ◆ (.skill-leak-sev, aria-hidden). The section already carries a ⚠ glyph + amber left border + amber heading + the explanatory note, so the per-row diamond restates 'this is a warning' a third time and competes with the mono skill name for the row's leading position. It carries no information the section header does not, and the diamond shape reads as a different severity vocabulary than the section's triangle. Severity is uniform ('warning') across all findings, so a per-row severity marker has nothing to differentiate.
findings.suggestedFix: Drop .skill-leak-sev so the skill name leads the row cleanly, OR if a leading marker is wanted for scannability use a neutral bullet (the muted ▸ used elsewhere in the drawer, e.g. citations) rather than a second amber severity glyph.

findings.title: Warning section is not announced as a status region to assistive tech
findings.detail: The <section class="skill-leak"> conveys 'warning' visually through amber + the ⚠ glyph, and in text through the note copy, so it is not colour-alone — that requirement is met. But the section has no accessible name or status semantics: the ⚠ is aria-hidden, and the heading is a plain <div>, so a screen-reader user lands on an unlabelled region and an unstructured 'Skill isolation (2)' line. This is consistent with the rest of the drawer (which also uses div eyebrows), so it is not a regression, just a missed opportunity on a surface whose entire purpose is to flag an anomaly.
findings.suggestedFix: Optional: give the section an aria-label (e.g. aria-label="Skill isolation warning") or add an sr-only "Warning:" prefix before the heading so the severity reaches non-visual users with the same emphasis the colour gives sighted ones.

findings.title: Roster head has no flex-wrap; long actor names plus the new leak chip can push the age chip
findings.detail: The new .agent-leak badge is flex:none and sits in .agent-head (display:flex, no flex-wrap, gap:6px). With a long actor name (which has no min-width:0 / overflow handling) plus role + state + runtime + skills + leak + age, the row can overflow and squeeze the trailing .agent-age. This is a PRE-EXISTING constraint the badge inherits — it correctly mirrors .agent-skills (same shape/sizing) and the leak case is rare (1 of 141 runs live) — so the badge does not introduce a new pattern. Flagging only because adding another flex:none chip to an already-tight, non-wrapping head incrementally raises the overflow risk.
findings.suggestedFix: No change required for this PR. If touched later, give .agent-name min-width:0; overflow:hidden; text-overflow:ellipsis (so it yields before chips do), or allow .agent-head to flex-wrap. Out of scope here since it is a roster-wide concern, not specific to the leak badge.

result.reasoning: The CSS facts in the finding are all accurate. `.agent-head` is `display: flex; gap: 6px; align-items: center;` with NO flex-wrap (app.css:142 and the duplicate at :281). `.agent-name` is `{ font-weight: 600; font-size: var(--fs-title); }` (app.css:143) with no min-width:0, overflow, or text-overflow, so it cannot shrink/ellipsize and holds its intrinsic width. The new `.agent-leak` (app.css:766) is `flex: none` and is byte-for-byte identical to `.agent-skills` (app.css:741) except color/background — so the finding's claim that the badge mirrors the existing skills chip is correct. The head markup (AgentRoster.svelte:50-68) places a `.spacer{flex:1}` (app.css:282) before the trailing chips, which absorbs slack; with a long actor name the spacer collapses to 0 and, because nothing in the row is shrinkable and there's no wrap, items can overflow and squeeze `.agent-age`. So the mechanism described is real. HOWEVER, this is explicitly a PRE-EXISTING roster-wide constraint: the leak badge introduces no new pattern, it exactly follows the established `.agent-skills` precedent that already sits in the same non-wrapping head. The finding itself concludes 'No change required for this PR', scopes the fix as out-of-scope (a roster-wide concern), and rates it nit. The leak case is also rare (1 of 141 runs live). Since the badge correctly mirrors existing precedent and the finding recommends no change here, it is not a genuine issue worth fixing in this PR — it is an accurate but non-actionable observation. Default isReal=false applies.
result.recommendedFix: No change for this PR. The leak badge correctly mirrors `.agent-skills` and inherits a pre-existing head-overflow constraint rather than creating one. If the roster head is revisited later as a dedicated cleanup, give `.agent-name` `min-width: 0; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis;` so the name yields before the trailing chips, or allow `.agent-head` to `flex-wrap`. Track it as a roster-wide polish item, not a blocker on this skill-leak surface.

result.reasoning: Confirmed from code. SkillIsolationFindings.svelte:35 renders `◆` as the leading element of every finding row, and app.css:775 styles `.skill-leak-sev { flex:none; color: var(--amber); ... }` — so it is an amber, severity-named marker. The finding's premises all check out: (a) the section already signals "warning" three other ways — a `⚠` glyph (line 21), an amber heading `.skill-leak-head` (css:769), an amber left border `.skill-leak` (css:768), plus the explanatory note (lines 24-27); (b) `SkillIsolationFinding.severity` is uniformly "warning", so a per-row severity marker differentiates nothing between rows; (c) the diamond `◆` is a different shape from the section's triangle `⚠`, introducing a second symbol into the same warning vocabulary; (d) being amber and first in `.skill-leak-row`, it sits ahead of the mono skill name (`.skill-leak-name`, line 36) which is the actual scannable identifier. The suggested neutral-bullet alternative is well-grounded: sibling citation lists in the very same drawer use a muted leading `▸` (InspectorDrawer.svelte:437, 658, 688), and skill rows use a leading `⚙` (SkillStacks.svelte:19) — so a per-row leading marker is idiomatic, but an amber *severity* marker is not the established choice. One nuance against over-weighting: `◆` is not reserved as a severity glyph here (SkillStacks.svelte:23 uses it as a neutral source-chip glyph), so it is not strictly a "different severity vocabulary" globally — but classed `.skill-leak-sev` and tinted amber it does read as severity in this local context. Net: a real, code-confirmed visual-noise observation, but purely cosmetic — aria-hidden, contrast passes, contract satisfied — hence a nit, not higher.
result.recommendedFix: Remove the `.skill-leak-sev` ◆ span at SkillIsolationFindings.svelte:35 (and its CSS rule at app.css:775) so the mono skill name leads each row cleanly — the section's ⚠ glyph, amber heading, amber left border, and note already establish the warning. If a leading marker is wanted for row scannability, replace the amber ◆ with the muted neutral `▸` already used by the citation lists in InspectorDrawer.svelte, styled with `color: var(--muted)` instead of `var(--amber)`, so it reads as a list bullet rather than a second, redundant severity signal.

result.reasoning:
Confirmed from the code. In SkillIsolationFindings.svelte the warning is rendered as `<section class="skill-leak">` (line 19) with no accessible name and no status role; the warning glyph is `aria-hidden="true"` (line 21) and the title is a plain `<div class="run-subhead skill-leak-head">` (line 20). So the two channels that signal "warning" to sighted users — amber colour and the ⚠ glyph — are both unavailable to AT (colour is inherently visual; the glyph is explicitly hidden). A screen-reader user lands on an unlabelled region and reads a bare "Skill isolation (2)".

The finding's own caveats are accurate and not inflated: this is NOT a WCAG 1.4.1 colour-alone failure, because the note copy (lines 24-27) carries the word "warning" in text, so the severity is still reachable by AT, just without upfront emphasis. The finding correctly self-rates nit.

Two corrections to the finding's framing, neither of which changes the verdict: (1) The fix is more idiomatic than "optional" implies — `.sr-only` already exists (app.css:27) and is used in Coverage/Specs/History, and the directly comparable WARNING surfaces in this same codebase already carry status semantics: Control.svelte uses `role="alert"` + aria-hidden glyph (lines 292-293), HumanActionDetail.svelte uses `role="note"` (line 299), Toaster.svelte wraps in `role="region" aria-label` (line 80). (2) The finding's "consistent with the rest of the drawer" defence does hold for the section HEADING specifically: the structural twin SkillStacks.svelte (the neutral Skills section this sits beside) uses the identical bare `<div class="run-subhead">` with no role (line 14), so a bare-div eyebrow is genuinely the house style for section titles. The gap is real but minor, and the contract does not mandate ARIA status semantics (it only requires not-colour-alone, which is satisfied).
result.recommendedFix:
Cheap, idiomatic improvement: give the section status semantics so the warning emphasis reaches non-visual users the way colour reaches sighted ones. Either add `role="note" aria-label="Skill isolation warning"` (or `role="status"`) to the `
`, or add an sr-only "Warning:" prefix inside the heading using the existing `.sr-only` class, e.g. `Warning: ` before the heading text. This matches the established pattern in Control.svelte / HumanActionDetail.svelte / Toaster.svelte. Not a blocker for merge.

result.summary: The implementation faithfully satisfies the substantive recommended-UI requirements of docs/architecture/skill-observability-ui-contract.md. Every contract field name is read correctly (eventStream.globalSkillReferences, diagnosis.failureClasses, the literal value "global_skill_leak", and run.skillIsolationFindings). global_skill_leak is correctly rendered as an amber, glyph-paired run-level WARNING (.reason-amber) and is explicitly NOT treated as a blocker — it is the only failure class special-cased to amber while genuine blockers (e.g. active_blocker) stay red. Missing skill data is uniformly NEUTRAL: every surface (roster badge, agent-detail section, focus-run section, and the shared component) is gated on length>0 and emits no error or empty-state noise. ANSI/VT escape stripping is applied before display via cleanLeakText, and the component is independent of the Skills binding so a leak surfaces even on runs with no managed packet. The full vitest suite (281/281) passes and the production build compiles clean (148 modules), confirming the {@const} runes placement is valid. Two issues remain, both below blocker level: (1) the contract's snapshot-section requirement "show a warning badge AND link to run focus" is met only indirectly — the badge links to agent detail (which does show the findings), but there is no path from the leak surface to the actual /api/focus/run/:runId packet where the run-level global_skill_leak warning and failureClasses live; (2) stale comments in skills.ts.

findings.title: Roster leak badge links to agent detail, not to the run-focus packet the contract names
findings.detail: Contract line 65 requires: "If skillIsolationFindings is non-empty, show a warning badge AND link to run focus." The amber .agent-leak badge is correct and its title says "open the agent to inspect," and clicking the agent card does open agent detail, which renders <SkillIsolationFindings findings={agentLeakFindings}/>. So the operator CAN reach the findings in one click — the spirit of the requirement is met. However, the literal target "run focus" is the /api/focus/run/:runId packet (the focusRun branch, lines 861-1032), where the run-level WARNING is shown via the failureClasses chip (global_skill_leak -> reason-amber) plus eventStream.globalSkillReferences. The leak surface offers no path there: focusRun is only reachable from the FocusRail (App.svelte:157) and the focusSlice "zoom into run" link (InspectorDrawer.svelte:842) — neither tied to a leak. The agent-detail isolation findings come from run.skillIsolationFindings, which is the same underlying data, so this is a path-completeness gap rather than a data gap.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a "zoom into run" affordance to the agent-detail Skill-isolation section (or to each run card) that calls store.select({ kind: "focusRun", id: run.id }) for the run carrying the finding, mirroring the existing focusSlice link at InspectorDrawer.svelte:842. That gives the operator the contract's explicit path from the badge to the run-focus packet where global_skill_leak is shown as a run-level warning.

findings.title: skills.ts comments claim the finding shapes are absent from the shared types.ts, but they are already declared there
findings.detail: skills.ts states the isolation-finding shapes are "NOT declared on the shared types.ts (user-owned)" and that accessors read run data "WITHOUT touching the shared AgentRunRecord type." That is now inaccurate: web/src/lib/types.ts:13 declares `export interface SkillIsolationFinding { kind: "global_user_skill_reference"; severity: "warning"; ... }`, line 14 adds `skillIsolationFindings?: SkillIsolationFinding[]` to AgentRunRecord, and lines 62/86 add `globalSkillReferences?: SkillIsolationFinding[]` to the focus shapes. The locally re-declared SkillIsolationFinding in skills.ts (kind/severity typed as plain string) is also a looser duplicate of the canonical typed one. This is purely a comment-accuracy / minor duplication issue — the defensive accessors still behave correctly and are arguably more robust against malformed live data — so it does not affect any contract requirement.
findings.suggestedFix: Either update the comments to reflect that types.ts now declares these shapes, or import SkillIsolationFinding from ~/lib/types and drop the local duplicate interface, keeping only the tolerant runtime accessors (skillsOf / normalizeFindings / isolationFindingsOf).

result.reasoning: Both cited locations are confirmed. SkillIsolationFindings.svelte:12-15 — snippetOf() does `clean.length > 160 ? clean.slice(0,159) + "…" : clean`, a JS 160-char cap with an appended ellipsis. app.css:779 — `.skill-leak-snippet { font-size: var(--fs-eyebrow); line-height: 1.4; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis; white-space: nowrap; }`, a single-line CSS clip. So the snippet is genuinely truncated twice. The render context is unambiguously narrow: the component is rendered only inside the InspectorDrawer (lines 592, 991), and `.inspector` is `width: 380px` (app.css:260) with --s3 (12px) padding plus the section's own --s3 padding, leaving roughly 330px of content width. The snippet is NOT monospace (only .skill-leak-name and .skill-leak-path set the mono family), at --fs-eyebrow 10.5px, so only ~55-60 characters fit on one line — far fewer than the 160-char JS budget. The finding's core technical claims are therefore accurate: with white-space:nowrap the JS 160 budget is never visible, the appended "…" from snippetOf is itself usually clipped, and the operator sees ~one line. This matters more than mere cosmetics because the snippet is the only contextual evidence in the warning, and — unlike .skill-leak-path which carries `title={path}` (line 39) — the snippet div (line 40) has NO title attribute, so the clipped remainder is unreachable even on hover. One nuance keeps this at minor, not major: the 160-char JS cap is not purely "dead effort" as the finding states — it is a legitimate defensive bound on DOM text-node size given snippets are scraped from raw ANSI PowerShell output that could be multi-KB; it just isn't doing visible-truncation work. Nothing is broken (no bug, renders fine, tests pass); this is a polish/UX-thinness observation, correctly scoped as minor and not inflated.
result.recommendedFix: Make the snippet evidence actually usable rather than redundantly clipped. Preferred: in app.css:779 drop `white-space: nowrap` and switch to a 2-line clamp — `display: -webkit-box; -webkit-box-orient: vertical; -webkit-line-clamp: 2; overflow: hidden;` — and raise/keep the JS cap (e.g. ~240) so two lines have content to fill. Also add `title={snippet}` to the snippet div (SkillIsolationFindings.svelte:40), mirroring the path's hover-reveal, so the truncated remainder is recoverable. Minimal alternative if a single line is intentional: delete the JS 160-slice in snippetOf() and let the CSS ellipsis own truncation (keep a generous defensive slice only to bound DOM size), and still add the title for hover-reveal. Either way, pick one visible-truncation strategy instead of stacking two.

result.reasoning: Confirmed from the actual code. `leakSkillName()` (web/src/lib/skills.ts:113-117) returns the last path segment via `clean.match(/[^\\/]+$/)`. The component renders that value as the row's lead token: SkillIsolationFindings.svelte:31 `{@const name = leakSkillName(f.path)}` then line 36 `{name || "(unknown skill)"}`. CSS confirms visual primacy: `.skill-leak-name` is `color: var(--ink)` (full primary text) + mono + `flex: none` (app.css:776), while the full path is demoted to `.skill-leak-path` at `--fs-eyebrow` (10.5px), `.muted`, single-line ellipsis (component line 39 + app.css:778), and is suppressed entirely when `path === name`. Codex skills are universally laid out `/SKILL.md` — the authoritative contract (docs/architecture/skill-observability-ui-contract.md, lines 156/163/167 and the focus-packet example at line 91) and src/skill-isolation.ts both show `.codex/skills/.../SKILL.md`. The unit test pins the broken behavior: skills.test.ts:152 asserts `leakSkillName(...project-overseer\\SKILL.md) === "SKILL.md"`, and the component test at line 200 asserts `getByText("SKILL.md")`. The single live run (RUN-c28d3b2f) carries 2 findings, both `project-overseer` SKILL.md references — so in production both rows lead with the identical, uninformative word "SKILL.md", while the actual identity (`project-overseer`) is buried in the muted ellipsised line below. The element given the strongest visual weight carries the least information; the squint test fails. This is a genuine information-hierarchy defect, not a false positive. I am dropping it from "major" to "minor" because: (a) the distinguishing folder IS still rendered (muted) on the path line, so the signal is recoverable, not lost; (b) this is a low-frequency warning surface (1 of 141 runs) that is explicitly never a blocker. One caveat in the data shape (paths "can be truncated mid-word") means a truncated path could end in a partial folder name rather than SKILL.md — in that case the current leaf is fine — but the documented/tested/live dominant case is the full `.../SKILL.md`, which is broken.
result.recommendedFix: Fix is helper-local in web/src/lib/skills.ts:leakSkillName — when the last cleaned segment is `SKILL.md` (or matches `^SKILL\.[^\\/]+$`, case-insensitive), climb to the containing folder and return that as the name (e.g. `project-overseer`), skipping dot-prefixed scaffolding dirs like `.system` if it is otherwise empty; fall back to the leaf when there is no usable parent. Keep the full cleaned path muted below for provenance (component needs no change). Update the two test assertions (skills.test.ts:152 and the component getByText at line 200) to expect the folder name. Optionally guard against truncated paths by only climbing when the leaf is a complete `SKILL.<ext>` match.

But web/src/lib/types.ts now declares all of these: line 13 `export interface SkillIsolationFinding { kind: "global_user_skill_reference"; severity: "warning"; path: string; snippet: string; lineNumber?: number; }`; line 14 adds `skillIsolationFindings?: SkillIsolationFinding[]` to AgentRunRecord; lines 62 and 86 add `globalSkillReferences?: SkillIsolationFinding[]` to the focus shapes. The per-run data is intact in resolvedRuns/agentRuns (each carries r.run.id; isolationFindingsOf(r.run) is per-run), so a per-run affordance is the precise target. result.recommendedFix: Add a per-run "zoom into run →" affordance on the run card(s) whose isolationFindingsOf(r.run) is non-empty, calling store.select({ kind: "focusRun", id: r.run.id }) — mirroring the existing focusSlice link at InspectorDrawer.svelte:840-844. findings.title: Slice-focus failure-class chips render global_skill_leak red instead of amber
findings.detail: The contract requires global_skill_leak to be a WARNING, never a blocker. The focusRun branch tints it amber at line 929, but the focusSlice Latest run chips at line 825 use unconditional reason-red for every failure class. lrfFailureClasses at line 782 comes from latestRunFocus.diagnosis.failureClasses and can include global_skill_leak, so the same class shows amber in run-focus but red in slice-focus. Impact today is low because the only live leak run is an overseer run with no slice, but any worker or reviewer leak would render red here, mis-signaling a reproducibility warning as a hard failure.
findings.suggestedFix: Apply the same conditional tint used at line 929: amber when the class is global_skill_leak, otherwise reason-red.

findings.title: leakSkillName returns the full path for paths ending in a separator
findings.detail: leakSkillName falls back to the whole cleaned string when there is no trailing non-separator segment, so a path ending in a slash returns the full path. Never throws and is purely cosmetic since the component also shows the full path and guards with an unknown-skill fallback, and real harness skill paths do not end in a bare separator. Verified harmless on live data.
findings.suggestedFix: Optionally strip trailing separators before extracting the last segment.

result.summary:
Logic is correct and robust, validated against the live RUN findings on disk. The accessor reads the exact field skillIsolationFindings; cleanLeakText strips live ANSI and control chars without eating normal text; the dedupe key matches the component each-key with no collision even where both live findings share line 5; the roster aggregates across all actorRuns and only badges when count is above zero; accessors are null-safe and never throw; the focusRun leakFindings const is a valid direct child of its if-block and reads eventStream.globalSkillReferences correctly. Production build compiles (148 modules) and svelte-check passes 0 errors. Vitest could not run locally due to an environment-level testing-library/svelte vs Vitest 4 incompatibility affecting all 26 test files, unrelated to this change; substituted build, svelte-check, and direct Node probes against live data. result.reasoning: Confirmed from the actual code. leakSkillName (web/src/lib/skills.ts:113-117) is: `const clean = cleanLeakText(path); const m = clean.match(/[^\\/]+$/); return m ? m[0] : clean;`. The regex `/[^\\/]+$/` is anchored to end-of-string and requires at least one non-separator char at the very end, so when the cleaned path ends in `/` or `\` it cannot match, m is null, and the function returns the full `clean` string. Verified empirically in node: `"/home/user/.codex/skills/foo/"` returns the full path instead of `"foo"`, while `"/home/user/.codex/skills/foo"` correctly returns `"foo"`. So the finding's core claim is accurate.\n\nThe finding's harmlessness assessment is also correct: (1) it never throws — pure string op with a fallback; (2) no data is lost. In SkillIsolationFindings.svelte the value flows to {@const name = leakSkillName(f.path)} (line 31), rendered at line 36 as `{name || \"(unknown skill)\"}`. When the bug triggers, name equals the cleaned path, so line 39's guard `{#if path && path !== name}` suppresses the redundant dedicated path line — the operator still sees the full path, just in the mono \"name\" slot, which is merely less tidy. The \"(unknown skill)\" fallback only fires on an empty name, not this case. (3) Real harness leak paths point at named files (the test at skills.test.ts:152 uses `...SKILL.md` → `SKILL.md`) and the one documented live finding (RUN-c28d3b2f) carries no bare-trailing-separator path; PowerShell mid-word truncation yields a partial segment that still matches the regex, not a trailing separator. The test suite (skills.test.ts:150-162) covers normal/no-separator/ANSI cases but not the trailing-separator edge. Genuine but purely cosmetic robustness gap; correctly the lowest severity.
result.recommendedFix: Optional, low priority. Strip trailing separators before extracting the last segment so a path ending in `/` or `\` still yields the skill name, e.g.: `const clean = cleanLeakText(path).replace(/[\\/]+$/, ""); const m = clean.match(/[^\\/]+$/); return m ? m[0] : clean;`. Add a test case (e.g. `leakSkillName(\"/home/x/.codex/skills/foo/\")` → `\"foo\"`) to lock it in. Not worth blocking the change; can be left as-is given it's harmless on real data.

result.reasoning: Verified directly in web/src/components/InspectorDrawer.svelte. Line 825 (focusSlice branch, "Latest run" block) renders failure-class chips with an UNCONDITIONAL static class: `{#each lrfFailureClasses as fc}{fc}{/each}`. By contrast, line 929 (focusRun branch, "Failure classes") uses the conditional tint: `{fc}`. So the identical class renders amber in run-focus but red in slice-focus. The data source is the same channel: line 782 `{@const lrfFailureClasses = strArr(pick(lrfDiag, "failureClasses"))}` where `lrfDiag = pick(latestRunFocus, "diagnosis")` (line 781). The authoritative contract docs/architecture/skill-observability-ui-contract.md line 85 states `failureClasses: string[]; // may include "global_skill_leak"` and line 105 requires: "If diagnosis.failureClasses includes global_skill_leak, show it as a run-level warning ... it is not automatically a slice blocker." Rendering it in `reason-red` (the failure/blocker color; app.css line 720 maps reason-red to --red) in the slice view mis-signals a reproducibility WARNING as a hard failure, contradicting the contract. Both `.reason-red` and `.reason-amber` exist (app.css 720-721), so the fix is well-supported. Severity "minor" is correct and not inflated: the finding itself honestly notes current live impact is nil (the only leak run, RUN-c28d3b2f, is an overseer run with no slice, so it never reaches this slice-focus "Latest run" code path), but any future worker/reviewer leak attached to a slice would render red here. It is a genuine consistency gap against the contract that the change set deliberately fixes at line 929 but missed at line 825.
result.recommendedFix: Mirror the line-929 conditional tint at line 825. Change `{#each lrfFailureClasses as fc}{fc}{/each}` to `{#each lrfFailureClasses as fc}{fc}{/each}`. This keeps the two failure-class render sites consistent and honors the contract requirement that global_skill_leak is a warning (amber), never a blocker (red). Consider extracting a small helper (e.g. failureClassTone(fc)) so future render sites can't drift again.
